title: Big four lenders bankroll Blackstone’s purchase of $36b HSBC loan book
full_text:
ANZ and NAB are among lenders bankrolling the $1.85 trillion private capital juggernaut Blackstone’s record-setting acquisition of HSBC Australia’s $36 billion book of home and personal loans.
Street Talk can reveal Blackstone has lined up $30 billion-plus in senior debt to pay what is the largest-ever sale of a bank’s mortgage book globally to a credit fund. ANZ and NAB are joined in the debt stack by BNP Paribas, Natixis, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, RBC Capital Markets and Standard Chartered, sources said on Sunday.
The loan has been structured as a privately offered residential mortgage-backed securitisation. Blackstone and its lenders are expected to put a public securitisation deal to credit funds and other institutional investors within a year of ownership, sources said.
Of note, it is understood Blackstone’s final offer was “very close” to the loan book’s $36 billion headline value, implying an equity cheque of less than $3.6 billion.
It comes as the RAMS portfolio, acquired last year from Westpac by a consortium comprised of KKR, PIMCO and Pepper Money , sold $15.38 billion worth of bonds under a prime RMBS issuance, dubbed Cashmere Funding 2026-1, on July 22. That deal is expected to serve as a blueprint for Blackstone’s strategy at HSBC in the coming months.
League tables glory for MS, Citi
Street Talk last week reported that Blackstone was closing in on HSBC’s Australian mortgage lending book, after nearly a year of talks with several major players, including NAB and Macquarie Bank. Blackstone was advised by Morgan Stanley, Barrenjoey and Mallesons, while Citi and Allens were on the sell-side.
Sources told this column that the sale process was initially hampered by a lack of interested parties with a retail banking licence, compounded by fears of client unrest amid an ownership change. HSBC ultimately withdrew the retail bank and, with just the mortgage book on offer, the global asset manager’s expertise and scale came up trumps.
Sources said two factors gave Blackstone the edge. First, the private capital giant does not have an Australian mortgage lending business, and faces a much easier road to securing approvals from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority as well as the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission – both of which have been tough on banks that are sitting on sizeable market share in mortgages.
Blackstone also did not have to worry about integrating HSBC’s book into an existing business, akin to ANZ’s $4.9 billion purchase of Suncorp Bank two years ago.
The deal, which is the biggest transaction to be announced in Australia in 2026, is expected to rewrite the M&A league tables. Citi and Morgan Stanley finished at No.4 and No.10 in the year to June 30, but have kicked off the new financial year with a bang.
